lesson.title: Mixed Together, Not Bonded: Understanding Mixtures
lesson.summary: This section contrasts mixtures with compounds, covers homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures, and surveys physical methods used to separate them.
lesson.body:
The previous section defined a compound as two or more elements chemically bonded together in a fixed ratio. A mixture is fundamentally different: it is matter formed when two or more substances are physically combined without any chemical bonding between them, so each substance keeps its own chemical identity and properties. Stir a spoonful of sand into a glass of water and you have a mixture. The sand grains are still silicon dioxide, and the water is still H2O; nothing about either substance has changed, they are simply sharing the same space. This is the key test for telling a mixture apart from a compound: in a mixture, you could in principle pick the components back apart using only physical methods, no chemical reaction required, and unlike a compound, a mixture's composition can vary freely. A cup of sweet tea can have a little sugar or a lot of sugar dissolved in it and still be called sweet tea; it does not have to match one fixed ratio the way NaCl always has to be 39.3 percent sodium by mass.

Mixtures are further divided into two categories based on how uniform they look and behave: homogeneous and heterogeneous. A homogeneous mixture, also called a solution, has the same composition and properties throughout, down to the molecular scale, so you cannot see distinct parts even under a microscope. Salt water is homogeneous: once the salt has dissolved, every sip tastes and behaves the same, because the sodium and chloride ions are spread evenly among the water molecules. Air is also a homogeneous mixture, mostly nitrogen and oxygen gas mixed uniformly with smaller amounts of argon, carbon dioxide, and water vapor. A heterogeneous mixture, by contrast, has visibly distinct regions or components with different properties. A salad, a bowl of granite chips, or a glass of water with sand settled at the bottom are all heterogeneous: you can point to one part and see it differs from another part nearby.

Because the substances in a mixture are not chemically bonded, they can usually be separated using physical processes that exploit differences in properties like boiling point, particle size, density, or solubility, the same physical properties covered in the next section of this unit. Filtration separates a solid from a liquid by passing the mixture through a barrier with holes too small for the solid particles to pass, which is how sand can be removed from sandy water. Distillation separates liquids with different boiling points by heating the mixture until the lower boiling substance evaporates first, then cooling that vapor back into a separate liquid, which is how fresh water can be recovered from salt water, since water boils at 100 degrees Celsius while the dissolved salt does not evaporate at all. Evaporation, simpler still, leaves dissolved solids behind once the liquid they were dissolved in has boiled or evaporated away, which is how salt is harvested from seawater in coastal salt flats.

Recognizing whether a sample of matter is an element, a compound, or a mixture, and if a mixture, whether it is homogeneous or heterogeneous, is one of the first skills a chemist develops, because it determines which tools and reasoning apply. A geologist analyzing a rock sample, a chef balancing a recipe, and a chemical engineer purifying a drug are all, in different ways, relying on this same classification system to decide whether they are working with a single pure substance or a combination that can be pulled apart.
